title: The OpenAI Agents SDK
summary: The OpenAI Agents SDK is a thin framework that owns the agent loop for you. You declare Agents (an instruction + a set of tools), plain Python functions become tools, agents hand off to other agents, a Runner drives the reason-act-observe cycle, and Sessions persist conversation state. It structures the loop so you write behavior, not plumbing — but the primitives (agent, tool, handoff, run) are the durable ideas, whichever library you end up using.

subtopics.title: An Agent is an instruction plus tools
subtopics.explanation: In the SDK an Agent is a small config object: a name, a system instruction describing its job, and a list of tools it may call. It is not the loop itself — it's the declaration of one participant's behavior. Defining agents this way is what lets the framework treat 'who is acting' as data it can swap and route between.
subtopics.example:
from agents import Agent

# an Agent is a declaration: name + instruction + tools
support_agent = Agent(
    name="support",
    instructions="You resolve billing questions. Be concise.",
    tools=[],  # filled in below
)
# nothing has run yet -- this just describes one actor in the system

subtopics.title: Plain functions become tools
subtopics.explanation: You mark an ordinary Python function with a decorator and the SDK reads its name, docstring, and type hints to build the JSON Schema the model needs. When the model requests that tool, the SDK calls your function with validated arguments and feeds the return value back as an observation. Turning functions directly into tools is why you spend time on logic instead of hand-writing schemas.

subtopics.title: Handoffs route work to another agent
subtopics.explanation: A handoff lets one agent transfer control to a more specialized agent, exposed to the model as if it were a tool it can call. The receiving agent takes over the conversation with its own instructions and tools. Handoffs are how the SDK expresses multi-agent routing, which is the same idea you build by hand in a router agent.
subtopics.example:
from agents import Agent

billing = Agent(name="billing", instructions="Handle refunds and invoices.")
tech = Agent(name="tech", instructions="Handle login and bug reports.")

triage = Agent(
    name="triage",
    instructions="Route the user to the right specialist.",
    handoffs=[billing, tech],  # triage can hand control to either
)
# the model 'calls' a handoff and control moves to that agent

subtopics.title: The Runner drives the loop
subtopics.explanation: Runner.run takes an agent and an input and executes the full reason-act-observe cycle: call the model, run any requested tools, apply handoffs, feed observations back, and stop when the agent produces a final answer. You do not write the while-loop yourself. The Runner is the framework's version of the agent loop you would otherwise hand-code.
subtopics.example:
import asyncio
from agents import Runner

async def main():
    result = await Runner.run(triage, "I was double-charged for May.")
    print(result.final_output)  # the Runner ran the whole loop for you

asyncio.run(main())
# no manual while-loop, tool dispatch, or handoff wiring needed

subtopics.title: Sessions persist conversation state
subtopics.explanation: A Session stores the running message history so successive Runner.run calls continue the same conversation instead of starting cold. You pass the same session across turns and the SDK appends each turn's messages automatically. Sessions are how a stateless model gets multi-turn memory, the same problem you otherwise solve by threading history through the loop yourself.
subtopics.example:
from agents import Runner, SQLiteSession

session = SQLiteSession("user-42")  # persists across turns

async def turn(text):
    r = await Runner.run(triage, text, session=session)
    return r.final_output

# await turn("I was double-charged")  -> handled
# await turn("and refund it")        -> remembers the prior turn

foundations.overview: The OpenAI Agents SDK is a small, opinionated framework that implements the agent loop so you declare behavior instead of writing plumbing. Its whole surface is a handful of primitives: an Agent (a name, an instruction, and a set of tools), function tools (plain Python functions whose signature and docstring become a JSON Schema automatically), handoffs (one agent transferring control to a specialist, exposed like a tool), the Runner (which executes the reason-act-observe cycle, running tools and applying handoffs until a final answer), and Sessions (which persist message history so multi-turn conversations continue seamlessly). The framework also layers guardrails and tracing on top. The key insight for an advanced engineer is that these are not proprietary magic — they are names for the loop, tools, routing, and memory you already understand. Learning the SDK is mostly learning where it draws its boundaries, so you can decide when its structure earns its keep versus when a stateful graph (LangGraph) or a hand-rolled loop fits better.
foundations.formalDefinition: The OpenAI Agents SDK is a Python framework whose core abstractions are: Agent (instruction + tool set + optional handoffs), function_tool (a decorator that derives a tool JSON Schema from a function's signature and docstring), handoff (a tool-like transfer of control from one agent to another), Runner (the executor that runs the model-tool-observation loop to termination), and Session (persistent conversation history). Runner.run orchestrates these into a complete agent execution.
foundations.whyItMatters: Hand-writing the loop, tool dispatch, argument validation, handoff routing, and history management is repetitive and error-prone. A framework that owns those concerns lets teams ship multi-agent behavior faster and more consistently, with built-in tracing and guardrails. Knowing the SDK's primitives — and their equivalents in other frameworks — is what lets you choose the right level of abstraction instead of defaulting to whatever you saw first.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the SDK as a stage manager for a play. Each Agent is an actor with a script (instructions) and props (tools). A handoff is one actor stepping aside and cueing another. The Runner is the stage manager who actually runs the show — feeding lines, fetching props, and calling the next actor — while you, the playwright, only write who does what. The Session is the memory of everything said so far, so the next scene follows from the last.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A triage agent that routes support tickets to billing, technical, or account specialists; a research assistant whose sub-agents search, read, and summarize; a coding helper that hands off between a planner and an executor; and internal tools where a lightweight framework beats a custom loop because tracing and guardrails come for free.
commonUseCases: Multi-agent triage and routing with handoffs
Turning existing Python functions into tools quickly
Multi-turn assistants needing persistent session memory
Prototypes where built-in tracing and guardrails save time

commonMisconceptions.myth: The SDK does something the raw loop can't.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It automates the same reason-act-observe loop you'd write by hand — model call, tool dispatch, observation, repeat. The value is convenience, consistency, tracing, and guardrails, not new capability.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A handoff spawns a separate parallel agent.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A handoff transfers control of the same conversation to another agent's instructions and tools; it's routing, not fan-out. Parallel sub-agents are a different pattern you build explicitly.

They target different needs. The SDK favors simple linear handoff flows with minimal code; LangGraph models explicit stateful graphs with branches, loops, and checkpoints. Pick by how much control over control-flow you need.

interactiveExamples.title: Triage with a handoff to a specialist
interactiveExamples.explanation: A triage agent inspects the input and hands control to the right specialist agent. The handoff is modeled as the Runner switching which agent's instructions and tools are active — the same conversation, a new actor.

code.caption: The handoff replaces the active agent mid-run; control, not just a message, moves to the specialist. The real SDK exposes each handoff to the model as a callable.

codeLab.title: Build a tiny agent runtime with tools and a runner
codeLab.instructions: Implement run_agent(agent, user_input, model) that reproduces the SDK's loop. The model is a callable that, given (instructions, history), returns either {"tool": name, "args": {...}} to call a tool or {"final": text} to stop. Your loop must: (1) call the model, (2) if it returns a tool call, look the tool up in agent['tools'] (a dict of name -> function), call it with the args, append the observation to history, and loop; (3) if it returns a final answer, return that text; (4) cap iterations at max_steps=5 and raise RuntimeError if exceeded. Complete run_agent so the harness passes.
hints: The loop has three moves per iteration: call the model (reason), run the requested tool (act), append its output to history (observe).
Check for a 'final' key first; if present, return immediately without touching tools.
Wrap the loop in `for _ in range(max_steps)` and raise RuntimeError after it if no final answer was produced.

debuggingLab.title: The handoff loses the conversation and loops forever
debuggingLab.symptom: A triage agent hands off to a billing agent, but the billing agent 're-triages' and hands right back — the two ping-pong until the step cap trips. Worse, when billing finally answers, it has no idea what the user originally asked because the handoff started a brand-new history.

brokenCode.code:
def run(agent, user_input, model, max_steps=6):
    history = [{"role": "user", "content": user_input}]
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        step = model(agent["instructions"], history)
        if "final" in step:
            return step["final"]
        if "handoff" in step:
            agent = step["handoff"]           # switch agent
            history = [{"role": "user",       # BUG: fresh history!
                        "content": user_input}]
            continue
        fn = agent["tools"][step["tool"]]
        history.append({"role": "tool", "content": fn(**step["args"])})
    raise RuntimeError("no convergence")

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Two coupled bugs. First, on every handoff the code throws away `history` and rebuilds it from just the original user_input, so the receiving agent loses all context gathered so far — it can't see that triage already classified the request, so it re-triages. Second, because nothing records that a handoff already happened, there's no guard against handing control straight back, so triage and billing bounce back and forth until max_steps. A handoff should transfer control while preserving the accumulated conversation, and repeated handoffs need a bound.
commonMistakes: Resetting the message history on a handoff instead of carrying it forward, so the new agent starts blind.
Treating a handoff as a fresh conversation rather than a change of the active actor within one ongoing run.
Not bounding handoffs (or the overall step count across agents), letting two agents ping-pong indefinitely.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Preserve the conversation across the handoff and prevent infinite re-routing. Keep the shared history, append a marker noting who took over, and cap the number of handoffs so a ping-pong can't run forever.

solution.code:
def run(agent, user_input, model, max_steps=6, max_handoffs=2):
    history = [{"role": "user", "content": user_input}]
    handoffs = 0
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        step = model(agent["instructions"], history)
        if "final" in step:
            return step["final"]
        if "handoff" in step:
            if handoffs >= max_handoffs:      # bound re-routing
                raise RuntimeError("too many handoffs")
            handoffs += 1
            agent = step["handoff"]
            # keep history; just note the transfer of control
            history.append({"role": "system",
                            "content": f"handed off to {agent['name']}"})
            continue
        fn = agent["tools"][step["tool"]]
        history.append({"role": "tool", "content": fn(**step["args"])})
    raise RuntimeError("no convergence")

theory.question: What are the core primitives of the OpenAI Agents SDK and how do they map to the raw agent loop?
theory.directAnswer: The primitives are Agent (instruction + tools), function tools (Python functions turned into schemas), handoffs (transfer of control to another agent), the Runner (the executor that drives the loop), and Sessions (persistent history). They map directly onto the hand-rolled loop: the Agent is the system prompt plus tool set, function tools are your tool dispatch table, handoffs are routing to another prompt/tool set, the Runner is the while-loop, and Sessions are the history you would otherwise thread through yourself.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A small framework that implements the reason-act-observe loop and multi-agent routing behind declarative objects, plus tracing and guardrails.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: So teams stop re-implementing tool dispatch, argument validation, history management, and routing for every agent, and get consistent observability for free.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You declare Agents with instructions and tools, decorate functions to expose them, list handoffs for routing, and call Runner.run with an optional Session; the Runner calls the model, executes tools, applies handoffs, feeds observations back, and returns the final output.

theory.whyImportant: Recognizing the primitives as names for concepts you already know lets you move between frameworks and choose the right abstraction level rather than being locked into one library's vocabulary.
theory.realWorldExample: A support triage agent lists billing and technical agents as handoffs; Runner.run classifies the ticket, transfers control to the specialist, and the specialist resolves it using its own tools — no hand-written loop or dispatch code.

followUps.question: Where does tool argument validation happen?
followUps.answer: The function_tool decorator derives a JSON Schema from the signature and type hints; the SDK validates the model's arguments against it before calling your function.

followUps.question: Is a handoff the same as calling a tool?
followUps.answer: It's exposed to the model like a tool, but instead of returning a value it transfers control of the conversation to another agent with different instructions and tools.

theory.question: When would you choose the OpenAI Agents SDK over LangGraph or a hand-rolled loop?
theory.directAnswer: Use the Agents SDK when your flow is mostly linear handoffs between a few agents and you want minimal code plus built-in tracing and guardrails. Use LangGraph when you need explicit control over branching, loops, parallelism, and durable checkpointed state — a graph you reason about as a state machine. Hand-roll the loop when your needs are simple or unusual enough that a framework's abstractions add more friction than they remove, or when you need full control with zero dependencies.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A selection decision across three levels of abstraction for orchestrating an LLM: a lightweight handoff framework, an explicit stateful graph framework, and a custom loop.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Different applications need different amounts of control over control-flow and state; matching the tool to that need avoids both boilerplate and over-engineering.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Judge by control-flow complexity and state needs: simple routing and quick delivery favor the SDK; complex branching, cycles, human-in-the-loop pauses, and persistence favor LangGraph; minimal or highly custom logic favors raw code.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing the wrong abstraction level is a common cause of unmaintainable agent code — either fighting a heavy framework for a simple task or hand-rolling fragile plumbing for a complex one.
theory.realWorldExample: A team prototyped a triage bot with the Agents SDK in an afternoon; when requirements grew to include conditional multi-step approvals with resumable state, they migrated the complex flows to LangGraph while keeping simple handoffs in the SDK.

followUps.question: What does LangGraph give you that the SDK doesn't?
followUps.answer: First-class explicit graphs with conditional edges, cycles, parallel branches, and checkpointed/persisted state you can pause and resume — control the SDK abstracts away.

followUps.question: Why ever hand-roll the loop today?
followUps.answer: For maximum control, zero dependency risk, unusual control-flow, or teaching/debugging clarity — the loop is only a dozen lines and every framework is just a wrapper over it.

scenario.question: Your team built a support bot on the Agents SDK. Product now wants a multi-step refund approval that can pause for a human, resume days later, and branch on the approver's decision. Do you extend the SDK app or change frameworks?
scenario.directAnswer: This new flow is a stateful, branching, pausable workflow — exactly what an explicit graph framework like LangGraph handles well and what the SDK's linear handoff model does not. Keep the existing simple triage/handoff flows on the SDK, but implement the refund-approval workflow as a LangGraph graph with a checkpointer so it can persist, pause at a human-approval node, and resume with the decision routing the next edge.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A migration/architecture decision triggered by a requirement (durable, resumable, branching workflow) that exceeds the abstraction the current framework provides.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The Agents SDK optimizes for quick linear handoffs and doesn't model long-lived pausable state or conditional multi-node graphs, so forcing it there means fighting the framework.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Model the workflow as nodes (submit, auto-check, human-approve, execute-refund) with conditional edges on the decision, back it with a checkpointer for persistence, and expose it behind the same interface so the rest of the app is unchanged; leave lightweight routing in the SDK.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows judgment about matching abstraction to requirements and avoiding the anti-pattern of bending a lightweight framework into a durable state machine.
scenario.realWorldExample: The team kept SDK-based triage for instant answers and built the refund approval as a checkpointed LangGraph flow; a paused approval survived a service restart and resumed correctly when the manager clicked approve two days later.

followUps.question: Could you have forced this into the SDK?
followUps.answer: Partly, by externalizing state yourself, but you'd be reimplementing a checkpointed graph on top of a framework not built for it — more code and more bugs than using the right tool.

followUps.question: How do the two frameworks coexist?
followUps.answer: Hide each behind a common service interface; the caller sends a request and gets a result, unaware whether an SDK handoff or a LangGraph workflow served it.

coding.question: Implement a minimal Runner that executes an agent loop with tool calls and a step cap, matching the SDK's reason-act-observe contract.
coding.thoughtProcess: The model is a callable returning either a tool request or a final answer. I maintain a history, loop up to max_steps, and on each iteration either return the final answer or dispatch the named tool from the agent's tool table, appending its output as an observation. I raise if the cap is hit without a final answer, mirroring how the real Runner bounds runaway loops.
lineByLine: history seeds the conversation with the user's input, exactly as the SDK does.
The for-loop bounds the run at max_steps so a non-terminating model can't loop forever.
model(...) is the reason step: it returns either a tool call or a final answer.
A 'final' key ends the run immediately, returning the answer to the caller.
Otherwise we look the requested tool up in the agent's tool table and call it (the act step).
The tool's return value is appended as a tool-role message (the observe step) so the next model call sees it.
Falling out of the loop means no final answer was produced, so we raise a bounded RuntimeError.
coding.timeComplexity: O(k) model/tool calls where k <= max_steps; per-step work is dominated by the model call.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(k) for the accumulated history of up to max_steps observations.

followUps.question: How would you add handoffs?
followUps.answer: Handle a 'handoff' branch that reassigns `agent` to the target while keeping `history`, and bound the number of handoffs to prevent ping-pong.

followUps.question: How would you persist across turns?
followUps.answer: Accept a session object, load its stored history at the start, and append this run's messages back to it at the end — the SDK's Session pattern.

keyTakeaways: The Agents SDK owns the loop: you declare Agents (instruction + tools) and the Runner drives reason-act-observe to a final answer.
Plain Python functions become tools via a decorator that derives the JSON Schema from the signature and docstring.
Handoffs transfer control of one conversation to a specialist agent — routing, not fan-out — and must preserve history and be bounded.
Sessions persist message history so successive Runner.run calls continue the same multi-turn conversation.
Pick by control-flow needs: the SDK for simple handoff flows, LangGraph for explicit stateful/branching graphs, raw code for minimal or unusual logic.
